\begin{abstract}
  In this research paper we will learn and investigate how various supervised learning models learn features. We will cover four path ways: Induction Biases, Domain Adaptation, Domain Generalization, and
  the Open Set Problem. The source code can be found on
  \href{https://github.com/ZainFarhan-Work/ATML}{GitHub} (https://github.com/ZainFarhan-Work/ATML).
\end{abstract}

% TODO: list the research questions of the four tasks here (manual: 'Introduction and research questions')
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

First, we will see the study the influence of Inductive Biases and Feature Representations, our goal here is to see the influence of model architecture.
By comparing the metrics of three well known and standard models (ResNet-50, ViT-B, CLIP). We will first perform a baseline metric on all of them, and then
perform 5 different experiments. Colour Bias, Grey Scale, Shape vs Texture, and Translation.

Then we will see Domain Adaptation and Domain Generalization, where we study DAN with MMD, DANN - Adversarial Alignment, CDAN, SAM, and DAN-DG. For the open set problem we will
see GCSC and PROSER with both MLS and Placeholder

\section{Experimental Setup/Methods}
\label{sec:setup}

All experiments use seed 6304. All deviations from the manual are in Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}.

\subsection{Inductive Biases and Feature Representations}
\begin{tight}
  \item \textbf{Dataset:} STL-10.
  \item \textbf{Models:} ResNet-50, ViT-B/16 and CLIP ViT-B-32, frozen, with linear heads (plus zero-shot CLIP).
  \item \textbf{Style transfer:} For Shape vs.\ Texture we used the AdaIN implementation, which follows \citet{huang2017adain}. The encoder/decoder architecture and the pretrained weights come from the public reimplementation \texttt{naoto0804/pytorch-AdaIN}, with weights mirrored at \texttt{BhupatiNadar/adain-style-transfer-models} on HuggingFace.
\end{tight}

\subsection{Unsupervised Domain Adaptation}
\begin{tight}
  \item \textbf{Data:} PACS. Source: Photo, Art Painting, Cartoon. Target: Sketch.
  \item \textbf{Model:} ResNet-18.
  \item \textbf{Optimisation:} AdamW, lr $10^{-4}$, wd $10^{-4}$.
  \item \textbf{Source-only:} Cross-entropy on the pooled source batch (also the ERM baseline for Task 3).
  \item \textbf{DAN} \citep{long2015dan}\textbf{:} $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{cls}+\lambda\,\mathrm{MMD}^2$ on 512-d features, kernel $=$ sum of 3 RBFs with bandwidths $\{0.5,1,2\}\times$ median pairwise squared distance of the combined batch (bandwidth detached), $\lambda=1$.
  \item \textbf{DANN} \citep{ganin2016dann}\textbf{:} gradient-reversal discriminator on the 512-d feature, $\alpha(p)=\frac{2}{1+e^{-10p}}-1$.
  \item \textbf{CDAN} \citep{long2018cdan}\textbf{:} as DANN, with discriminator input $\mathrm{vec}(f\otimes p)$.
\end{tight}

\subsection{Domain Generalisation}
\begin{tight}
  \item \textbf{ERM:} shared with Task 2. No Sketch access.
  \item \textbf{DAN-DG:} $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{cls}+\frac{\lambda_{DG}}{3}\sum_{e<e'}\mathrm{MMD}^2(F(X_e),F(X_{e'}))$, $\lambda_{DG}=1$.
  \item \textbf{SAM} \citep{foret2021sam}\textbf{:} $\min_\theta\max_{\lVert\epsilon\rVert_2\le\rho}\mathcal{L}(\theta+\epsilon)$, $\rho=0.05$.
  \item \textbf{Sharpness proxy:} $\Delta_{\mathrm{sharp}}=\mathcal{L}(\theta+\epsilon)-\mathcal{L}(\theta)$, $\epsilon=0.05\,g/\lVert g\rVert_2$.
\end{tight}

\subsection{Open-Set Recognition}
\begin{tight}
  \item \textbf{Data:} CIFAR-10 train 50,000 $\to$ stratified 90/10: 45,000 train / 5,000 val. Testing was done on both CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (near and far unknowns, 800 each).
  \item \textbf{Model:} CIFAR ResNet-18: $3\times3$ stride-1 stem, no max-pool, random initialisation, $32\times32$ input, 512-d feature, Linear(512,10).
  \item \textbf{GCSC:} vanilla recipe plus RandAugment (2, 9).
  \item \textbf{PROSER} \citep{zhou2021proser}\textbf{:} initialised from Vanilla, 5 dummy classifiers, $\beta=1$, $\gamma=0.1$.
  \item \textbf{Scores:} MSP \citep{hendrycks2017msp} $=1-\max_k p_k$. MLS \citep{vaze2022osr} $=-\max_k z_k$. Energy \citep{liu2020energy} $=-\log\sum_k e^{z_k}$. Mahalanobis $=\min_c (f-\mu_c)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(f-\mu_c)$.
  \item \textbf{Threshold:} 95th percentile of the score on CIFAR-10 validation.
\end{tight}

\label{sec:results}

All the models perform well as a baseline, this maybe a limitation of the STL-10 dataset, as its distinct classes would be easier to classify.


\subsubsection{Color Bias}

We did two experiments with colour, the first we changed the images to greyscale measured the same metrics and got the following results (Table~\ref{tab:grayscale}).

% [moved to appendix, Task 1 / Color Bias: tab:grayscale]

We can see that making the image greyscale results in a slight decrease in accuracy throughout. A more interesting observation is that there was no significant difference between Convolution and Vision Transformers, 
though consistency is slightly higher for the Vision Transformer. CLIP had the most sever impact. Both of the readings are lower than either
ResNet or ViT-B, and further zero-shot is the lowest.

The second experiment was with a Hue Shift of $40^{}$ deg.

% [moved to appendix, Task 1 / Color Bias: tab:hue40]

Again we see a minimal change in accuracy (Table~\ref{tab:hue40}), this time they are much closer to each other. No claims can be made as the difference is small enough that it can
be considered noise. It is also of note that unlike greyscale, CLIP is
much more in line with other models.

\subsubsection{Shape vs. Texture}

For this comparison alpha strength of 1 was required. We get the following results:

\begin{table}[tb]
  \caption{Shape vs Texture: Convoutional models are not shape biased.}
  \label{tab:shape-texture-both}
  \centering
  \footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{lcccrrrr}
    \toprule
    & \multicolumn{5}{c}{Balanced ($n=220$)} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{All accepted ($n=286$)} \\
    \cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(lr){7-8}
    System & $N_{\text{sh}}$ & $N_{\text{tex}}$ & $N_{\text{oth}}$ & Shape bias & Coverage & Shape bias & Coverage \\
    \midrule
    ResNet-50 + linear head     &  54 & 52 & 114 & 50.94 & 48.18 & 57.78 & 47.20 \\
    ViT-B/16 + linear head      &  99 & 14 & 107 & 87.61 & 51.36 & 89.94 & 55.59 \\
    CLIP ViT-B-32 + linear head & 116 & 12 &  92 & 90.62 & 58.18 & 91.72 & 59.09 \\
    CLIP ViT-B-32 zero-shot     & 117 &  7 &  96 & 94.35 & 56.36 & 95.81 & 58.39 \\
    \bottomrule

\begin{figure}[tb]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{figures/cue_conflict_examples.png}
  \caption{Example Images}
  \label{fig:cue-conflicts}
\end{figure}

Out of a total of 400 candidate images only 286 were of good enough quality, which were further reduced to 220 to make each class balanced.
As expected, the Vision Transformers have a considerable shape bias, while the convolutional model does not. Though one point of note is that
ResNet still managed to score a 50.94 on the Shape Bias. This is considerably higher than the original \citet{geirhos2019texture} paper. The reason for this
can be mostly likely presumed to be the biggest limitation of this experiment.

That is that the images were filtered out manually. This introduced significant human bias in the process making the data unreliable.

Another notable observation is that for ViT and ResNet both, there most quantitative category is neither shape nor texture, and CLIP barely has more shape classified images.
Making the coverage very low, and limiting our ability to draw further conclusions from this data.

% (T1-RQ1): colour + cue-conflict jointly
Together it is clear that colour reliance is very low, and cue conflict shows us that shap and texture reliance is high by comparison.. However the low coverage makes
further analyses and stronger claims difficult.

\subsubsection{Patch Structure + Translation}

We divided the images into 4x4 patches, and shuffled the patches. We feed the shuffled images back in the model to measure the metrics (Table~\ref{tab:patch-shuffle}).

% [moved to appendix, Task 1 / Patch Structure: tab:patch-shuffle]



The ViT-B and ResNet model are close in accuracy.

One final thing of note is that CLIP performs noticeably worse than ViT, even though they share the visual encoder (as a Vision Transformer), the fact that both zero-shot and linear head land at the same number
implies that its not the involvement of the text encoder in the prediction process. This suggest that contrastive learning (with the text encoder) during pre training or some other stage had some factor that made
them more dependent factor.\footnote{We also saw more shape bias for them in table~\ref{tab:shape-texture-both}, but it was not enough of a difference to warrant any conclusion}

% (T1-RQ2) translation + patch shuffle 
The data for Translation can be seen in Figure\ref{fig:translation}, from that it is clear that the spatial order is much more vital to the model than simply moving the image.

In terms of grayscale and translation we can see the Norm is rather high. This is consistent with our earlier hypothesis that
models don't look at colour for classification.

In Patch shuffling the values a bit lower (around 0.6). What is more interesting is that CLIP and ViT show a large difference despite
them both having a Vision Transformer. One plausible explanation is that since CLIP's tokens are twice as wide as ViT, they are more dependent on global
structure, and the representation drifts more. This becomes more apparent in the following diagram.

% (T1-RQ3,RQ4): prediction vs representation agreement/mismatch
Overall, a representation changes doesn't always men a prediction change. FOr greyscale they all have roughly the same Norm, but there is a noticeable difference between model performance, with ViT being the most stable.
We've seen that though model architecture is not the full story  as the two CLIP which are close still showed some variance in results (shape bias is 90.6 vs 94.4), it is still largely important, as ViT and CLIP were very shape biased, while CNN was not.

\subsection{Unsupervised Domain Adaptation}

\subsubsection{Source Only ERM}

We first train both the model and the classifier hear on the source domains using cross entropy, which results in these measurements (Table~\ref{tab:source-only}).

% [moved to appendix, Task 2 / Source Only ERM: tab:source-only]

As we can see in source only statistics, the accuracy on our source domains is very good, but when ran on a unknown domain (for us that is sketch) we notice a massive accuracy drop.
compared with the mean it is a -33 points drop.

% [moved to appendix, Task 2 / Source Only ERM: tab:source-only-per-class]

when we see the by class accuracy on the target domain (Table~\ref{tab:source-only-per-class}), dog performs worst while elephant performs best.
Dog is one of the largest class in the sketch data, we found dog's 333 most common errors go to elephant, 167 to giraffe. It is probable it is not confusing
animals and objects at least, it is confused within animal classes.

\subsubsection{DAN - MMD Alignment}

% [moved to appendix, Task 2 / DAN - MMD Alignment: tab:dan]

If we observe the general by class results for MMD, we see a slight but still meaningful improvement over the sketch accuracy (Table~\ref{tab:dan}).
Though the sketch F1 - macro decreases by a bit.

% [moved to appendix, Task 2 / DAN - MMD Alignment: tab:dan-per-class]

We see all classes improve in accuracy, except for giraffe and elephant (Table~\ref{tab:dan-per-class}).

\subsubsection{DANN - Adversarial Alignment}

We now use adversarial learning to see how well it performs. And get the following results (Table~\ref{tab:dann}).

% [moved to appendix, Task 2 / DANN - Adversarial Alignment: tab:dann]

Interestingly not only is the performance on the sketch pictures worse than source, but the the predictions on source only is also worse.
At first this might make it look like DANN didn't work, but after further investigation we find this (Table~\ref{tab:dann-training}).

% [moved to appendix, Task 2 / DANN - Adversarial Alignment: tab:dann-training]

The Loss was indeed decreasing, and the Domain Accuracy was going to 0.5., what this means is that even if we fool the discriminator.
that does not necessarily mean an increase in performance.

% (T2-RQ4): expectation for lambda before results
As alignment rises, the data converges and separability is reduced while sketch accuracy is improved a little. moderate alignment is helpful but too much destroys class information.
we can use Macro-F1 without target labels as a signal.
\subsubsection{Controlled Design Study}

\begin{table}[tb]
  \caption{Control study - too high a $\lambda$ collapses the model}
  \label{tab:t2-study-compact}
  \centering
  \footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{lccc}
    \toprule
    $\lambda_{\mathrm{MMD}}$ & Mean source F1 (\%) & Sketch acc.\ (\%) & Domain separability (\%) \\
    \midrule
    0 (source-only) & 94.85 & 61.59 & 100.00 \\
    0.1             & 94.73 & 62.31 &  92.17 \\
    1               & 94.93 & 64.44 &  81.87 \\
    10              &  5.07 &  4.07 &  60.03 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

A higher $\lambda$ means a higher penalty for difference between the source domain feature distribution.  $\lambda = 10$ completely collapses the model. F1 Mean on source alone is enough to disqualify 10 as optimial even without
consulting target domain labels.

% (T2-RQ1..3): gap size + worst classes; separability vs target; CDAN vs marginal (fig training-curves)
We had Source-only reach 94.91\% mean source accuracy against 61.59\% on Sketch, a drop of 33.3 points. We saw that lower separability does not mean better prediction on target domain. And we saw class conditioning massively help
in target domain accuracy.
\subsection{Domain Generalization}

We ruse the same ERM Baseline as last time, refereed to in table~\ref{tab:source-only}.

\subsubsection{DAN-DG - Pairwise Source-Domain Alignment}

In our initial configuration, which matched task with DAN for the sake of comparison, the model collapses (Table~\ref{tab:dandg}).

% [moved to appendix, Task 3 / DAN-DG - Pairwise Source-Domain Alignment: tab:dandg]

We speculate that this happens due to the model too aggressively trying to align the source domains (Table~\ref{tab:dandg-collapse}). So to remedy this we try
to ramp up the penalty term ($\lambda$) from zero to one as the model trains instead of just starting from one (Table~\ref{tab:dandg-variants}).

However this didn't work, that was visible from source-side metrics alone with source F1 5.07, feature std 0, MMD 0 by epoch 4. So as a last resort we increase the Bandwidth Gradient to 1 in the RBF Kernel,
this finally results in a significant improvement to the sketch accuracy, however we can no longer
compare these results to our earlier experiments.

% TODO(T3-RQ2): DAN-DG separability drop vs Sketch gain; evidence of lost class information (per-class table t2-per-class)

DAN-DG did make source domains less distinguishable but that was not tha main driver for improvement in sketch accuracy. The model completely collapsed with $\lambda = 1$.

We compare all our numbers against each other, with one interesting trend that was also in Domain Adaptation, which that accuracies on source domains
are not at all predictive of  sketch accuracy, difference between source being minimal with SAM and ERM only, but sketch accuracy is massively improved by SAM.

We see that DAN-DG does the most work for Source Domain Separability which is what MMD targets, while SAM does not really touch for domain separability but does reduce sharpness the most as we want it to.
SAM performs very well compared to DAN.


% (T3-RQ1,RQ3,RQ4): mean/worst source vs Sketch; sharpness ranking vs Sketch ranking; DAN (Task 2) vs DAN-DG (Task 3) and its limits
We now have also seen that mean source and and worst source are not good indicators or predictors of performance on the target domain (sketch). SAM lowers the sharpness the most, but that only
partly tells us how well the model will perform on sketch. It is also hard to tell whether target aware DAN or target free DAN is better.
The best target-aware result (CDAN, 74.65) is essentially tied with the best target-free one (SAM, 74.12). DAN and DAN-DG have difference that makes the scenario less comparable. DAN-DG tries to bring
sources together, while DAN brings source and target together. The final DAN-DG also lets gradient flow through the kernel bandwidth, while DAN keeps it detached, so the kernels aren't identical.

Detecting Far imges seems to be much easier throughout.
In table~\ref{tab:osr-failures} we can see that where as the worst Near are all wrongly classied at above 80\%, the far are all less than 60\%.

% TODO(T4-RQ1..4): plausible vs surprising failures + absorbing classes; what each score captures; GCSC near vs far; PROSER trade-off; AUROC vs 95% operating point
We saw it is much easier to accept near vs far, 555 of 800 near unknowns are accepted (69\%), against 363 of 800 far (45\%). Pickup truck, bus, and wolf got accepted most for near,
while wardrobe, mushrooms, and sunflower for far. pickup -> automobile, bus -> truck, tractor -> truck, wolf -> dog were plausible failures while Wardrobe -> cat, mushroom -> cat and sunflower -> bird were surprising.
MSP is normalised confidence and discards logit magnitude. MLS and Energy keep magnitude. Mahalanobis uses feature-space distance, so it is the most independent signal.
MLS and Energy were close to each other, and MSP were close to both, with Mahalanobis being furthest. We saw very good improvements from GCSC, while little difference from PROSER in near rej (PROSER was worse for far rej).
\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We saw that in terms of inductive bias, CNNs have strong texture bias (compared with ViT or CLIP) while Visual Transformers have a shape bias. Neither had strong colour or translation Bias.
For Domain Adaptation we see DAN with MMD beat DANN with adversarial alignment while CDAN did better than both. WIth DOmain Generalization we saw SAM
perform better than DAN-DG as well as being much more stable. Lastly, with our Open Set problem we saw GCSC significantly out perform, while both PROSER variants
were unable to beat even vanilla

\section{Deviations and Caveats}
\label{app:deviations}
\begin{tight}

\item \textbf{Mirrors.} STL-10 verified byte-identical; PACS and CIFAR mirrors could only be checked by counts (class and domain totals).
\item \textbf{Task 2 discriminator lr} $10^{-3}$ vs the specified $10^{-4}$ (adversarial methods only).
\item \textbf{Task 3 DAN-DG headline} uses the bandwidth-gradient MMD, which differs from Task 2's DAN implementation; the as-specified collapse is documented. A like-for-like comparison would re-run Task 2's DAN with the same flag.
\item \textbf{Task 3 separability probe} is class-weighted but not count-balanced across the three domains (manual: ``balanced features'').
\item \textbf{Task 4} augmentations run on uint8 tensors, not PIL; crop and flip are identical, RandAugment resampling can differ in rounding. PROSER losses were checked against the paper's Eq.\ 4, 5 and 7, not against the authors' code.
\end{tight}

\section{Table Notes}

\textbf{Table~\ref{tab:task1-compact}.} Top-1, macro-F1 (F1), $\Delta$ Top-1 and consistency (Cons.) in \%; Conf.\ is mean
  max confidence. $\Delta$ and Cons.\ are relative to each system's own clean predictions. CLIP is
  OpenCLIP ViT-B-32; the other systems use linear heads on frozen features.

\textbf{Table~\ref{tab:t2-diagnostic}.} Sep.\ = domain separability: held-out accuracy of a logistic-regression probe
  ($C=1$, balanced, 70/30 split, seed 6304) trained to tell source from target from the frozen
  features. Chance is 50\%. Target labels were used only at this stage.

\textbf{Table~\ref{tab:osr-scores}.} Test accept.\ is the share of CIFAR-10 test images accepted at the threshold.

\textbf{Table~\ref{tab:osr-models}.} CSA is closed-set accuracy on the ten known-class logits, so both PROSER rows share
  it. Test accept.\ is the share of CIFAR-10 test images accepted at the threshold.

\textbf{Table~\ref{tab:osr-failures}.} Vanilla, MLS; accept when the score is $\le\tau$. Each row is the most confidently
  accepted image of that unknown class; the last column gives how many of its 100 test images
  were accepted.

\textbf{Table~\ref{tab:t3-common}.} ERM is Task 2's source-only checkpoint, reused unchanged. SAM uses the specified
  $\rho=0.05$. DAN-DG uses $\lambda_{\mathrm{DG}}=1$ with gradient flowing through the
  median-heuristic bandwidth; with the bandwidth detached the run collapsed
  (Table~\ref{tab:dandg-collapse}).

\textbf{Table~\ref{tab:t3-common}.} Separability: three-way logistic-regression probe over Photo / Art Painting /
  Cartoon on frozen features, $C=1$, 70/30 split, seed 6304; chance is 33.3\%.
  $\Delta_{\mathrm{sharp}}$: cross-entropy increase after one normalised ascent step of radius 0.05
  on a fixed batch of 32 images per source domain, model in eval mode.
